issues.legal_issue: A statutory authority operating under a special summary eviction procedure cannot condone delay in filing the affidavit seeking leave to defend when the procedure fixes a filing deadline and grants no power to extend it.
material_facts: The eviction proceeding was brought under a special summary procedure for recovery of possession from a tenant or licensee.
The summons was served, but the occupant did not file an affidavit seeking leave to defend within the prescribed period; an earlier application to summon a document did not seek leave to defend.
The Competent Authority condoned the delay and later granted leave to defend.
The special procedure prescribed the steps and consequences for seeking leave, and did not confer power on the Competent Authority to extend the filing period.
issues.conclusion: The Competent Authority had no power to condone the delay or grant leave on the late application. The High Court correctly set aside those orders, and the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: The special procedure in Chapter VIII of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999, particularly Sections 39 and 43(4), governs the Competent Authority and overrides inconsistent provisions of other laws. The Authority is a statutory, quasi-judicial authority whose powers are confined to those conferred by the statute; deeming it a civil court for limited purposes does not make it a court for all purposes or attract the Limitation Act, 1963. A statutory authority has no inherent power to condone delay. The Court distinguished the treatment of courts in Mukri Gopalan v. Cheppilat Puthanpurayil Aboobacker and P. Sarathy v. State Bank of India, and considered Sakuru v. Tanaji, Birla Cement Works v. G.M. Western Railways, France B. Martins v. Mafaida Maria Teresa Rodrigues, Thakur Jugal Kishore Sinha v. Sitamarhi Central Co-operative Bank, and Gurditta Mal v. Bal Swarup; it rejected reliance on inherent powers under Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for this statutory authority.

rule.if: summary_eviction_proceeding and summons_duly_served and defence_leave_affidavit_filed_after_deadline and procedure_fixes_filing_deadline and authority_has_no_power_to_extend_deadline

predicates.summary_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction under a special summary procedure.
predicates.summons_duly_served: The person defending the eviction proceeding was duly served with summons.
predicates.defence_leave_affidavit_filed_after_dead: The person filed the affidavit seeking leave to defend after the applicable filing deadline.
predicates.procedure_fixes_filing_deadline: The governing procedure requires an affidavit seeking leave to defend to be filed within a specified period.
predicates.authority_has_no_power_to_extend_deadlin: The authority deciding the proceeding was not given power to extend the specified filing period.

issues.definition: When a person duly served in a summary eviction proceeding files the required defence affidavit late under a procedure that sets a deadline and gives the authority no extension power, the late application cannot be condoned.

issues.legal_issue: A selected candidate does not acquire an indefeasible right to appointment when an employer bona fide decides not to fill all advertised vacancies for appropriate reasons and no rule requires all vacancies to be filled.
material_facts: A bank had submitted a larger initial vacancy indent and later reduced it before the selection results were published.

The bank relied on financial and operational constraints, including losses, liquidity difficulties, and increased establishment costs, and the Court found the reduction bona fide and supported by appropriate reasons.
The candidates had been selected, but the governing recruitment scheme and rules did not require the bank to fill every vacancy or appoint every selected candidate.
The bank had no vacancies in the relevant cadres at the time of the Court's decision and had been identified as having surplus manpower.
issues.conclusion: The candidates had no indefeasible right to appointment, and the bank had no legal duty to fill all the vacancies. The appeals were allowed and the High Court judgments were set aside. The Court nevertheless directed that, if business needs required further appointments and the candidates' turns arose according to merit, they be considered for absorption under the rules; the select list was to remain in force for the period directed by the Court.
issues.legal_principle: Under Shankarsan Dash v. Union of India, a successful candidate ordinarily has no indefeasible right to appointment, and an employer need not fill all vacancies unless the applicable rules so require. A decision not to fill vacancies must be bona fide and for appropriate reasons, and an employer that does fill vacancies must respect comparative merit and avoid discrimination. The Court also relied on Union Territory of Chandigarh v. Dilbagh Singh, State of Andhra Pradesh v. V. Sadanandam, Babita Prasad v. State of Bihar, State of Haryana v. Subash Chander Marwaha, and U.P. Bhumi Sudhar Nigam Ltd. v. Shiv Narain Gupta. The applicable recruitment rules did not require all selected candidates to be appointed, and the Government of India guidance of 31 March 1993 contemplated revised indents and alternative arrangements for unabsorbed candidates.

predicates.recruitment_selection_case: The dispute concerns candidates selected through a recruitment process who seek appointment.
predicates.employer_reduced_vacancies_before_result: The employer reduced the number of vacancies it sought to fill before the selection results were published.
predicates.employer_had_bona_fide_appropriate_reaso: The employer's decision not to fill all vacancies was made bona fide for appropriate reasons.
predicates.no_rule_requires_all_vacancies_to_be_fil: The governing recruitment rules do not require the employer to fill every vacancy or appoint every selected candidate.

issues.definition: In a recruitment selection case, candidates have no indefeasible appointment right when the employer reduces vacancies before results for bona fide appropriate reasons and no governing rule requires all vacancies to be filled.

issues.legal_issue: A candidate cannot claim an appointment entitlement from the appointment of a lower-ranked candidate in another employer's selection when the recruitment and merit lists are employer-specific and no lower-ranked candidate was shown to have been appointed by the candidate's employer.
material_facts: Candidates applied for a particular regional rural bank, and the recruitment materials restricted each candidate's choice to one bank.
The results were declared for individual banks rather than through a common merit list applicable across all banks.
No factual foundation was laid to show that the bank had appointed a lower-ranked candidate from the same selection while denying appointment to a higher-ranked candidate.
The High Court's contrary view rested on an assumption that there was a common merit list across the banks.
issues.conclusion: The assumption that candidates could claim appointment based on a lower-ranked candidate's appointment by another bank was erroneous. The relevant selection and merit comparisons were bank-specific, and the High Court's contrary ruling was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Shankarsan Dash v. Union of India establishes that a candidate ordinarily has no indefeasible right to appointment, while requiring comparative merit to be respected if vacancies are filled. The Court applied that principle to the recruitment materials, which restricted candidates to a single bank and showed that results were bank-specific. A comparative-merit claim therefore required a factual basis showing that the same bank appointed a lower-ranked candidate over the claimant.

predicates.recruitment_selection_case: The dispute concerns appointment after a recruitment selection.
predicates.selection_and_merit_lists_are_employer_s: The recruitment process assigns candidates and ranks them separately for each employer.
predicates.alleged_lower_ranked_appointment_was_by_: The appointment relied on as evidence of unfair treatment was made by an employer other than the one from which the claimant seeks appointment.

issues.definition: When recruitment and merit lists are employer-specific, an appointment by another employer does not create a comparative-merit entitlement against the claimant's employer.

issues.legal_issue: A non-speaking dismissal of an earlier special leave petition does not establish the correctness of the challenged decision as precedent and need not be treated as a ruling on the legal issue.
material_facts: The bank relied on an earlier special leave petition concerning a similar dispute that had been dismissed without reasons.
The respondents argued that the earlier dismissal and the bank's failure to disclose it barred the later appeals.
The earlier dismissal order contained no reasons.
issues.conclusion: The non-speaking dismissal did not amount to acceptance of the correctness of the decision challenged in that petition and did not constitute law declared by the Supreme Court. The Court held that the earlier dismissal need not have been disclosed in the later petitions.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 141, a non-speaking dismissal of a special leave petition does not lay down law or signify acceptance of the correctness of the decision sought to be appealed. The Court relied on Kunhayammed v. State of Kerala.

predicates.later_appeal_case: The court is deciding a later appeal concerning a legal dispute.
predicates.earlier_special_leave_petition_dismissed: An earlier special leave petition concerning the dispute was dismissed without reasons.

issues.definition: In a later appeal, an earlier special leave petition dismissed without reasons has no precedential effect.
